title: The Woman Who Kept Gaining Weight — Obesity, Breathlessness, and a Voice That Changed at Night

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
She is 59 years old. Looking back, she traces the start of her weight problem to her first pregnancy, at age 24, a year after she married — she gained weight then and never fully lost it. A second pregnancy eight years later added more, even though, oddly, that baby was born underweight (not premature, just small). From that point on, her weight climbed steadily. Not in dramatic jumps, she says, just a slow, relentless increase, year after year, until her BMI passed 40.

Five years ago, two things happened close together: she was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, and she had cataract surgery in both eyes, a month apart. Her vision has been good since.

Then, about three weeks before she came in, something shifted. She started her diabetes medication and, paradoxically, gained 8–9 kg in just 20 days — from roughly 88 kg to 97 kg. She also cut back on sweets and sugar during this time, though the rest of her diet stayed the same, and she says she actually eats very little. Urination has been normal throughout.

In the last 10–15 days, she has started having trouble breathing. Her lifestyle, by her own description, is not very active. She has snored for 10–15 years and occasionally talked in her sleep, quietly. But in the last two weeks, both have intensified sharply — she is now snoring loudly and talking a great deal in her sleep, in a much louder voice, according to her family.

Also in the last 10–15 days, she has developed multiple mouth ulcers and feels that the right side of her face is swollen.

And there is one more piece that puzzles everyone, including her: despite needing insulin, despite eating, she keeps having hypoglycemia — low blood sugar even after meals.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- **HbA1c:** within normal range
- **ENT evaluation:** Mallampati grade 2, with the soft palate not visible at all — a red flag for a crowded airway
- **Abdominal imaging:** grade 2 fatty liver changes

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
As the team observed her over the following days, new findings emerged that reshaped the picture:

- A sleep study (polysomnography) was ordered, given the loud snoring, witnessed sleep talking, and Mallampati 2 airway — raising strong suspicion for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).
- Despite a documented normal oxygen saturation, she developed an altered sensorium — disorientation, agitation, and irrelevant speech — prompting a psychiatry consult. She was started on aripiprazole for this psychosis.
- The team began to wonder whether her clinical picture — central weight gain, fatigue, skin/mouth changes, and glucose instability — could reflect hypercortisolism, especially since it emerged that she had reportedly been taking unknown Ayurvedic medications on her own for years, possibly containing steroids, without her family's knowledge. A 24-hour urinary cortisol was planned to investigate this, but was ultimately not completed.
- Because the exact content of the unknown medications she was taking could not be verified (chemical analysis of unregulated preparations is not available at most centers), the team could not confirm or rule out exogenous steroid exposure as a contributor to her metabolic and psychiatric picture.
- Her psychosis gradually improved, and she was preparing for discharge.
